suggestions.assertion: The tutor gives the learner a real integration-by-parts problem to attempt and asks to see their work, rather than solving it for them up front.
suggestions.reason: The learner's own message already says 'дай мне задачу и посмотри, как я её решаю' (give me a problem and watch me solve it) — a tutor with no skill and no file access would very likely comply with this explicit instruction anyway. This assertion mainly checks basic instruction-following, not skill-specific behavior; it would probably pass in a no-skill baseline too.

suggestions.assertion: No complete worked solution to the specific problem posed is disclosed before the learner has made an attempt.
suggestions.reason: Same concern as above: since the learner explicitly asked to be given a problem and observed while solving it (rather than shown a solution), almost any reasonable assistant response — skilled or not — would withhold the solution here. This is a weak discriminator for whether the exam-prep skill's attempt-first/H0 policy specifically was applied, versus generic politeness/instruction-following.

suggestions.assertion: The tutor does not impose the ticket_list-specific 'brief answer structure' checkpoint or 'unprompted reproduction from memory'/'delayed recall' framing on this problem_set request — it uses the intuition-to-transfer problem ladder (or an equivalent worked/faded/guided approach), not the recitation track.
suggestions.reason: This is a compound assertion bundling two distinct checks (absence of ticket_list-style recitation framing, and presence of the correct problem_set ladder). Both happened to hold here, but if only one had held the grader would have to make an arbitrary call on how to score it. Consider splitting into two separate assertions for cleaner signal in future runs, especially runs where a track-selection bug is suspected.

No assertion checks whether the tutor's chosen problem difficulty/type is actually appropriate for an 'unseen' target under the problem_set ladder (i.e., that a diagnostic-stage problem, not an advanced/transfer-stage one, was chosen). Here ∫x·cos(x)dx is a reasonable moderate first example, but a run that gave an unreasonably hard or trivial first problem for an unseen concept would still pass all six current assertions.

No assertion checks that the reply is not just grounded in local state but also correctly interprets it — e.g., that the tutor did not silently mis-state a status field. This transcript's claims all check out against the reported CLI output, but the eval only has the transcript's own narration of tool output to grade against (no raw workspace JSON was included in outputs_dir), so a subtly fabricated 'status output' embedded in the transcript would be difficult for a grader to catch without independent access to the workspace files.

eval_feedback.overall: All six expectations pass with genuine, traceable evidence (the tutor ran `status`/`next`, correctly read question_model to select the problem_set ladder over ticket_list, and grounded every specific claim in that tool output rather than fabricating history). The two solving-related assertions (giving a problem instead of a solution) are only weakly discriminating here because the learner's own phrasing already dictated that behavior — they would likely pass without the skill too. The state-reading and track-selection assertions (1, 3, 5, 6) are the ones actually doing the work of distinguishing skilled from unskilled behavior in this eval.
